chapter_theme: Two songs at Singai (சிங்கை, given with Kangeyam, காங்கேயம்): pleas to be freed from trusting women and wandering shamelessly after them, with praise of the vel, of Valli, and of Siva's dance that bowed Kali's head.

937.reading: The poet says that, drawn by women's hair where bees hum among cool lilies and by their pearl-hung breasts like hills, he came trusting as refuge a poisonous deed and a desire for a woman; he asks Murugan today to destroy his evil deeds and come on the peacock. The praise names the vel fragrant with lotus, konrai, thumbai and magizh flowers, the vel that fought while goblins feasted on corpses, the chest that embraced the Kura girl of fine speech, and the lord at Singai of shining champak groves.
937.nuance: தஞ்சமென வந்து நம்பி: he sought the woman as a refuge (தஞ்சம்), the word devotion reserves for the Lord. The line ending கதிர்வேலா is used twice in the praise, which may be a slip in the source.

938.reading: The poet asks whether he must wander shamelessly at every crossroads, heart withered, with the belly as his only aim, and asks for grace so that, no longer roaming under the sway of women, his deeds may leave him and his mind be glad. The praise names Murugan son of Siva with the crescent on his hanging matted hair, who danced to the drum syllables until Kali, the woman of battle, bowed her head, the one who married the hunters' daughter, threw the vel at the asuras, and is son of Kampar and of the lord of Kailasa, at Singai.
938.nuance: சந்திதொறு நாணமின்றி: shame lost at every crossroads is the confession; உந்தி பொருளாக may mean living for the belly or for the women's navel. மங்கை ரணகாளி தலைசாய points to Siva's dance contest with Kali, in which she yielded; கம்பர் names Siva of Kanchi.
